name: Electronic Health Records
description: Iran’s electronic health record landscape includes national hospital-data exchange through SEPAS and primary-care documentation through SIB. Research shows why collecting records, making systems usable, and delivering demonstrable benefits to patients require separate evaluation. [s1][s2]

seo.title: Electronic Health Records in Iran: SEPAS, SIB and Data Exchange
seo.description: Understand Iran’s hospital and primary-care record systems, their different functions, and research on usability and interoperability.

content.heading: Understanding SEPAS
content.content:
An electronic health record collects patient information digitally so that it can support care beyond an isolated paper document. In Iran, a central initiative is SEPAS, the national electronic health record project developed under the Ministry of Health and Medical Education. A study published in 2023 describes hospital information systems transferring demographic details, diagnoses, procedures, investigation results and billing information through nodes hosted by medical universities to ministry databases. This describes an exchange architecture; it does not establish that every patient has a complete, continuously accessible clinical history. [s1]

The distinction matters because a repository can accumulate information without becoming a tool routinely used at the bedside. In the study’s 2021 setting, SEPAS primarily stored hospital encounter information, and physicians and nurses were not its direct users. Health information management personnel handled transfers. The researchers’ evaluation raised concerns about stability and patient-care benefits, showing why technical coverage and practical usefulness should be assessed separately. [s1]

content.heading: SIB and everyday primary care
content.content:
Primary care has a different documentation environment. SIB, the Persian abbreviation used for the Integrated Health System, was designed to collect community and primary-care information as a basis for electronic records. Its functions include documenting demographics, screening, immunization, diagnoses and prescriptions. A 2024 research article reports that it had been in use since 2015. These functions should not be confused with proof of seamless exchange between SIB, hospitals and every other service. [s2]

The same article examined childcare documentation in health centres affiliated with Kashan University of Medical Sciences. During fieldwork in 2020, providers completed realistic tasks while explaining their actions aloud. Researchers identified problems including information entry spread across multiple pages and recommendations that did not fit the task appropriately. Such findings reveal how the design of a record system can consume staff attention during a consultation. They concern selected tasks in a local study, rather than all SIB functions or its condition at the editorial cutoff. [s2]

content.heading: Why shared definitions matter
content.content: Interoperability also depends on agreement about what a field means. Research conducted in 2015 and published by the World Health Organization in 2020 examined Iranian hospital records, software documentation and SEPAS materials to develop a minimum data set. Its administrative and clinical categories illustrate the work needed before information from different systems can be compared reliably. The publication presents a proposed data specification, rather than evidence that every hospital subsequently implemented it. [s3]

name: Hospital Management Systems
description: Hospital management systems connect administrative and clinical information within a hospital. Iranian research highlights the importance of shared data definitions, usable interfaces and reliable integration across departments. [s1][s2]

seo.title: Hospital Management Systems in Iran: Workflows and Usability
seo.description: Explore Iranian hospital information systems, from shared clinical data to emergency workflows, implementation challenges and software transitions.

content.heading: The information behind hospital operations
content.content:
Hospital management systems are often discussed in Iranian research as hospital information systems, or HIS. Their information extends across administrative and clinical work. A national minimum-data-set study examined hospital records and software documentation to identify common information requirements, distinguishing administrative data from clinical documentation. The study demonstrates why a hospital needs shared definitions as well as computer terminals: information must remain understandable when it moves between departments or is used for reporting. Its proposed specification should not be read as proof of universal implementation. [s1]

The practical question is whether software supports the work being performed. An emergency department, for example, needs information that staff can enter and retrieve while responding to unpredictable admissions. A system’s presence alone says little about how well that workflow functions. [s2]

content.heading: What frontline evaluations reveal
content.content:
Research published in 2023 examined emergency information systems in public teaching hospitals in Kerman, drawing on nurses’ and information-technology staff members’ experiences. Reported problems included repeated manual documentation, difficulty finding patients, system crashes and absent decision support. Some accounts also described gaps between hospital software and departmental equipment or radiology processes. These are local findings, rather than a national failure rate. [s2]

Their wider significance is methodological: evaluation should follow an actual task through the system. A record that can technically be saved may still require duplicate entry or leave staff searching for information. The Kerman study therefore helps explain why users’ accounts are important alongside assessments of software features. [s2]

content.heading: Implementation involves people and institutions
content.content: An Iranian study published in 2024 identified social and technical obstacles to electronic-health implementation, including training costs, security concerns, platform diversity and difficulty integrating software into daily work. It also assessed hospital cases using the Electronic Medical Record Adoption Model, a framework for examining digital maturity. Findings from those cases cannot establish the maturity of every Iranian hospital. They nevertheless show why purchasing software is only part of implementation: staff preparation and organizational change also affect whether it becomes useful. [s3]

content.heading: New platforms still need scrutiny
content.content:
A study published in 2026 examined the transition from the desktop-based IHIS platform to the web-based Sepid platform at Qaem Hospital in Mashhad. It focused on admission and radiology, combining expert inspection with user assessment. Sepid received more favourable usability evaluations, but both platforms retained important weaknesses. Reported concerns included responsiveness, error feedback, navigation and integration with external databases. [s4]

This comparison offers a useful conclusion for understanding hospital modernization: a newer interface can improve experience while leaving substantial workflow problems unresolved. Because the study concerned a single teaching hospital and selected modules, it supports careful local evaluation rather than a nationwide ranking of products. [s4]

name: Telemedicine
description: Telemedicine in Iran includes patient-facing online consultation and remote consultation between clinicians. Research documents practical services alongside persistent questions about integration, professional preparation, financing and governance. [s1][s2][s3]

seo.title: Telemedicine in Iran: Online Care and Specialist Consultation
seo.description: Understand Iran’s remote consultation models, evidence from the Moein programme, and research on access, integration and implementation barriers.

content.heading: Different ways to deliver care at a distance
content.content:
Telemedicine uses communication technologies to deliver clinical services across distance. In Iran, it encompasses different relationships: a patient may consult a clinician through an online platform, while a doctor may seek specialist input about a patient already receiving local care. These models have different information needs and should not be treated as one uniform service. Iranian research examines both patient-facing online consultation and structured consultation between physicians. [s1][s2]

The distinction also helps explain apparently conflicting descriptions of implementation. A review published in 2025 characterized telemedicine as insufficiently embedded in formal services, but its evidence search covered studies only through March 2022. Later research describes an operational specialist-consultation programme. The older review is therefore evidence about implementation barriers, rather than a definitive inventory of services at the editorial cutoff. [s2][s3]

content.heading: Specialist advice through the Moein programme
content.content:
A 2026 study examined Iran’s Moein programme, which supported obstetrics and gynaecology consultation between physicians. In the setting studied during 2023–2024, referring and consulting clinicians discussed cases through live voice calls. Interviews highlighted information gathering, interpretation of the situation, shared decisions, ethical and emotional factors, and available resources. [s2]

The study makes clear that remote expertise depends on communication as well as connectivity. The consultant needs a useful account of the patient’s condition, while the referring clinician must interpret advice within the local clinical setting. This qualitative investigation explains participants’ experience; it does not establish a reduction in complications or prove that the model performs equally well across specialties. [s2]

content.heading: Online consultation and continuity of care
content.content:
Research published in 2025 explored policymakers’ and administrators’ views of online medical consultation using interviews conducted in 2024. Participants saw potential advantages in access, follow-up and reduced travel burdens. They also described practical tensions: text conversations could take substantial time, clinicians needed preparation for remote practice, and platform services were not consistently integrated with established care pathways. These are stakeholder assessments, rather than measured national savings or clinical effects. [s1]

For readers assessing digital care, integration is a central question. The existence of an online encounter does not itself demonstrate that its information reaches the patient’s other providers. The study accordingly identifies connections with national information systems and clearer implementation arrangements as priorities. [s1]

content.heading: What the evidence can establish
content.content:
The broader review grouped Iranian implementation barriers around governance, financing, the workforce and health information systems. A separate interview study with health policymakers similarly identified policy weaknesses, unclear operating mechanisms and difficulties changing established service models. Together, these sources explain why telemedicine cannot be understood simply as installing a communications application. [s3][s4]

The evidence supports a measured conclusion: remote consultation has documented uses in Iran, while sustainable expansion depends on organizational arrangements and professional practice. Claims about nationwide coverage, universal insurance reimbursement or improved population outcomes require additional evidence beyond these implementation studies. [s1][s2][s4]
